method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from French Reference Center for Hypereosinophilic Syndromes (CEREO), Groh M, Rohmer J, Etienne N, et al., Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases 'French guidelines for the etiological workup of eosinophilia and the management of hypereosinophilic syndromes' (published 30 April 2023), 33 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10148979). S2: QUOTED from Leukemia and Lymphoma Group, Chinese Society of Hematology, Chinese Medical Association, Zhonghua Xue Ye Xue Za Zhi (Chinese Journal of Hematology) 45(1):1-7 (doi 10.3760/cma.j.cn121090-20231222-00334) '中国嗜酸性粒细胞增多症诊断和治疗指南（2024版） [Guideline of the diagnosis and treatment of eosinophilic disorders in China (2024)]' (January 2024), 11 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 3.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC10951113). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every CEREO 2023 claim (S1) unchanged and adds S2, the Chinese Society of Hematology 2024 national guideline (CC BY 3.0, quoted), for work-up steps, emergency steroid dosing, imatinib escalation and maintenance, targeted options for FGFR1, JAK2, ABL1 and FLT3 fusions, and second-line agents for idiopathic HES. S2 is written in Chinese: its fragments are stored in Chinese and the English claims are the verifier's own translation. The number guard cannot see a numeral written directly against Chinese characters (it counts them as part of a word), so where the source numeral is joined to Chinese text the claim spells the number out; those numbers were checked by hand. Searched and not usable: BSH 2017 eosinophilia guideline (Br J Haematol, subscription), ESC Heart Failure Association 2026 clinical consensus statement on heart involvement in eosinophilia (Eur J Heart Fail, subscription), NCCN 2021 M/LN-eo guideline (not open access). The ICOG-EO 2023 criteria paper (Allergy, CC BY) is readable but covers classification, not treatment. No Australian HES guideline or eviQ protocol was found. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S1 Boxes 2 (clinical manifestations), 3 (HE-inducing drugs), 4 (investigations for persistent HE), 6 (organ-specific eosinophilic disorders), 8 (imatinib), 9 (pegylated interferon) and 10 (hydroxycarbamide). Most of these boxes are two-column lists, so the extractor reads their first entry as a column heading; the row lines are still verbatim. S1 Box 1 (definitions; merged cells), Boxes 5 and 7 (lymphocytic HES versus angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma; HES versus EGPA; ragged rows) and S2 Table 1 (merged cells) were not extracted.

claims.claim: **Definitions:** eosinophilia is 0.5-1.5 per nL; hypereosinophilia (HE) is above 1.5 per nL and/or tissue eosinophilia. HES is diagnosed as soon as HE is judged to cause organ dysfunction, whatever the cause.
claims.source_text: this classification distinguishes blood eosinophilia (between 0.5 and 1.5 × 109/L eosinophils), HE (blood eosinophilia > 1.5 × 109/L and/or tissue eosinophilia) … the diagnosis of HES is made as soon as blood and/or tissue HE is found to be the cause of clinical organ dysfunction (regardless of the underlying mechanism/etiology of HE)

claims.claim: **The eosinophil count does not track severity**; organ damage depends on tissue infiltration and eosinophil activation. With urgent, life-threatening disease, a 1-month wait before diagnosing HES is no longer required.
claims.source_text: Generally, there is no correlation between the level of blood HE and the severity of clinical manifestations (which is more closely related to the extent of eosinophilic tissue infiltration and the degree of eosinophil activation within tissues). … a minimal delay of 1 month is no longer required before the diagnosis of HES can be retained.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Emergencies:** eosinophilic myocarditis, intracardiac thrombus with embolism, severe asthma or hypoxic lung disease, strokes and arterial or venous thrombosis. A very high count alone (for example above 10 per nL) without clinical involvement is not an emergency.
claims.source_text: These mainly include cardiac manifestations (e.g., eosinophilic myocarditis, intracavitary thrombosis with peripheral or cerebral embolic events, coronary artery spasm, acute heart failure), respiratory disorders (severe acute asthma or hypoxic lung disease), central nervous system manifestations (typically strokes of bilateral watershed distribution) and thrombotic (either arterial or venous) events … Contrariwise, in the absence of overt clinical manifestations, very high eosinophil counts (e.g., > 10 × 109/L) are not per se an indication for emergency initiation of treatment.

Hypereosinophilic asthma with nasal polyps is usually airway-limited type 2 disease but can be part of HES.

claims.claim: **The GP starts the work-up** (history, examination, first-line tests for drug and parasitic causes), but must refer to an organ specialist without delay for unusual symptoms or suspected cardiac, respiratory, thrombotic or neurological disease.
claims.source_text: A general practitioner or pediatrician who will conduct a history-taking interview and perform a comprehensive physical examination (possibly supplemented by basic first-line investigations) to screen for the most common causes of HE (drug-related or parasitic infection, as detailed in "Pharmacological treatments" section) and potential related complications. This initial workup must not delay the referral to an organ specialist physician if there are any unusual symptoms or if serious (cardiac, respiratory, thrombotic, neurological) disease is suspected.

claims.claim: **For recent-onset HE above 1.5 per nL, look first for drugs and parasites.** Drug-induced HE usually appears 2-8 weeks after starting the drug; common culprits include NSAIDs, antiepileptics, antibiotics, sulfonamides and allopurinol. Stop the suspect drug where possible.
claims.source_text: In the presence of recent onset HE > 1.5 × 109/L: etiologic investigations should focus on drugs and parasites … The duration of HE (and the temporal relationship between its onset and the initiation of a drug, typically 2-8 weeks) is an important consideration. Likewise, the history of previous CBC can be instructive. The main drug classes that are routinely implicated in HE are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antiepileptic drugs, antibiotics, sulfonamides and allopurinol … Whenever in doubt (and whenever possible), an attempt to discontinue the potential culprit drug/product should be performed.

claims.claim: **Suspect a clonal (myeloid) cause** with hepato- or splenomegaly, cytopenia, thrombocytosis, polycythaemia, monocytosis, basophilia, raised vitamin B12 or tryptase, or eosinophils that do not normalise on steroids. Endomyocardial fibrosis, border-zone strokes and mucosal ulcers point strongly to FIP1L1::PDGFRA disease, which is mainly seen in men.

A dose of 100 mg daily is sufficient to achieve a complete response, while improving tolerability … The introduction of imatinib may be recommended even before the result of the FIP1L1::PDGFRA test when the patient's condition is severe, and the clinical and laboratory findings are suggestive of such diagnosis. claims.claim: ⚠️ **Imatinib monitoring (same S1 box):** watch for musculoskeletal pain, gut upset, photosensitivity, cytopenias, oedema, abnormal liver tests and, in children, slowed growth; check bloods every 2 weeks for the first 2 months, then every 3 months. Pause treatment for toxicity such as neutrophils below 1.0 per nL, platelets below 50 per nL or transaminases above 5 times the upper limit. If anti-HBc is positive, check HBV viral load at the start and twice a year (reactivation, sometimes fulminant, has been reported).
claims.source_text: The main potential adverse reactions are musculoskeletal pain, gastrointestinal disorders, photosensitivity, cytopenia, edema, abnormal liver function tests and growth retardation in children. These adverse reactions should be screened for at each follow-up visit and call for require regular laboratory monitoring (e.g., every 2 weeks for the first 2 months, and then every 3 months thereafter). In case of laboratory abnormalities suggestive of imatinib toxicity (e.g., severe neutropenia < 1.0 × 10 9 /L, thrombocytopenia < 50 × 10 9 /L, cytolysis >5ULN, etc.), temporary cessation of therapy is recommended. Finally, since cases of viral reactivation (sometimes with fulminant hepatitis) have been reported in HBV-positive patients treated with imatinib, HBV viral load monitoring is recommended at the start of treatment and semiannually thereafter in patients with anti-HBc antibodies.

claims.source_text: When imatinib is co-administered with other drugs, drug interactions may occur. In particular, imatinib is a substrate for s -glycoprotein and is metabolized by cytochrome 3A4 (CYP3A4); caution should therefore be exercised when imatinib is prescribed in combination with CYP3A4 inducers (including rifampicin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and phenytoin), CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, azole drugs, macrolides, amiodarone, diltiazem, vancomycin, etc., risk of decreased effectiveness of imatinib), CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, azole drugs, macrolides, amiodarone, diltiazem, verapamil, etc., increased risk of adverse reactions from imatinib), or with other CYP3A4 substrates with a narrow therapeutic margin (e.g., anticalcineurins, sirolimus, warfarin and other coumarin derivatives, and digoxin).

claims.claim: **Corticosteroids are first line** and usually work quickly. Prefer local steroids where possible; when systemic treatment is needed use prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day, then taper to the lowest effective dose. In chronic disease about 12 months of treatment is advised before trying to stop.
claims.source_text: Corticosteroid therapy is generally the first-line treatment for idiopathic HES, and rapid response (complete or partial) is the norm. … The loading dose (0.5-1 mg/kg/day prednisone (off-label)), possibly preceded by pulses of methylprednisolone (15 mg/kg/day for 1-3 days) in case of organ- or life-threatening manifestations, should be tailored to the severity of symptoms before gradual tapering. Overall, the minimum effective dose should be used, and weaning should always be discussed: in acute forms, cessation of corticosteroid therapy may be attempted after a few weeks of treatment; in the case of chronic disease, a treatment period of approximately 12 months seems advisable before considering cessation.

claims.source_text: It is therefore standard practice to start with the lowest possible dosage (e.g., 45 µg pegylated interferon alfa-2a weekly by subcutaneous injection) and to increase it gradually monthly if necessary, depending on tolerability. … In practice, it is usually started at a low dosage (1 g/day in a single dose) and then increased if necessary (up to 2 g/day in a single dose) depending on effectiveness and tolerability … imatinib (400 mg/day) may also be used empirically (and off label) in patients with laboratory and clinical findings suggestive of underlying myeloid malignancies (although by definition, idiopathic HES does not show the cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities characteristic of clonal HES) e.g. splenomegaly, elevated vitamin B12 or tryptase, presence of other CBC abnormalities, nonresponse to corticosteroid therapy (or corticosteroid dependence on more than 10 mg/day prednisone) []. In the absence of response at 1 month after initiation of imatinib, the latter should be discontinued and replaced by another steroid-sparing drug.

claims.claim: **Pegylated interferon alfa-2a (S1 Box 9):** weekly subcutaneous injection, starting low in HES (for example 45 μg a week, less than for myeloid neoplasms or hepatitis), with paracetamol 1 g every 8 hours for 24–48 hours to reduce flu-like symptoms. Monitor full blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, transaminases and TSH; in cytopenia, space the injections and/or lower the dose.
claims.source_text: [Box 9 row 1] Pegylated interferon alfa-2a is administered by weekly subcutaneous injections. In HES, common practice is to start with low doses (e.g., 45 μg per week, less than those used for myeloid neoplasms or viral hepatitis) to promote tolerability and long-term adherence. Combination with prophylactic administration of paracetamol (1 g every 8 hours for 24-48 hours) should be offered to reduce flu-like symptoms that can sometimes be observed after injection. … In addition, regular laboratory monitoring (including CBC, serum electrolytes, creatinine, transaminases, TSH) is recommended. In the event of cytopenia, the intervals between injections of pegylated interferon alfa-2a may be increased and/or the dosages reduced.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Pegylated interferon contraindications (same S1 box):** children under 3, benzyl alcohol hypersensitivity, severe decompensated liver failure, platelets below 100 per nL, and progressive autoimmune disease (especially lupus, dermatomyositis, other interferon-mediated disease and autoimmune hepatitis); weigh any past autoimmune disease case by case. With a history of mood or personality disorder, see a psychiatrist first, as it can cause mood disorders.
claims.source_text: Pegylated interferon alfa-2a is contraindicated in children under 3 years of age, in case of documented hypersensitivity to benzyl alcohol, severe decompensated liver failure, thrombocytopenia < 100 × 10 9 /L or progressive autoimmune disease (particularly systemic lupus erythematosus, dermatomyositis, other diseases mediated by interferon pathways and autoimmune hepatitis). Overall, if there is a history of preexisting autoimmune disease, the benefit/risk ratio of treatment with pegylated interferon alfa-2a should be weighed on a case-by-case basis. In patients with a history of mood and/or personality disorders, a psychiatrist should be consulted prior to initiation of treatment (and monitoring increased if necessary), as this drug may induce mood disorders.

claims.claim: **Hydroxycarbamide (S1 Box 10):** 15–30 mg/kg a day orally in one or two doses; in HES start low (for example 1000 mg daily) and increase as needed, while emergency starts are typically 1500–2000 mg daily. Not for pregnancy, lactase deficiency or severe cytopenia (platelets below 100 per nL, haemoglobin below 10 g/dL); use with caution after radiotherapy or chemotherapy, and reduce the dose in renal failure or with other myelosuppressants. Hydrate at the start if HE or splenomegaly is marked or uric acid is high.
claims.source_text: [Box 10 row 1] Hydroxycarbamide is administered orally at a daily dosage of 15-30 mg/kg (in one or two daily doses). Outside of emergency settings (where the starting dose is typically 1500-2000 mg daily), the standard practice for HES is to start with a low dosage (e.g., 1000 mg daily) and then increase it as needed depending on treatment effectiveness and tolerability. Hydroxycarbamide is contraindicated in patients with lactase deficiency, pregnancy and severe cytopenia (neutropenia < 10 × 10 9 /L, thrombocytopenia < 100 × 10 9 /L and/or anemia < 10 g/dL).: Because the risk of bone marrow failure is higher in patients who have received prior radiation or chemotherapy, hydroxycarbamide should be administered with caution in this situation. Likewise, in case of renal failure and/or concomitant use of other myelosuppressive agents, a reduction in the dosages of hydroxycarbamide and increased monitoring are recommended. … In case of significant HE, significant splenomegaly and/or elevated uric acid levels, hydration is recommended at the start of treatment to prevent the possible occurrence of lysis syndrome.

claims.claim: **Hydroxycarbamide monitoring (same S1 box):** clinical and laboratory checks every two weeks for two months, then every three months, looking for mouth or light-induced skin lesions, skin atrophy or cancer and fibrosing lung disease. Mean red-cell volume can rise to 120 fL. No live attenuated vaccines while on it.
claims.source_text: Regular (e.g., every two weeks for two months after initiation of treatment, and then every three months thereafter) clinical (including screening for oral or photo-induced lesions, trophic skin disorders, skin neoplasia and/or fibrosing lung disease that may be promoted by treatment) and laboratory monitoring (including CBC, serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine, transaminases, etc.) is indicated in long-term treatment. Hydroxycarbamide treatment is known to be associated with an increase of erythrocytes' average globular volume of to up to 120 fL. Lastly, live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in case of concomitant treatment with hydroxycarbamide.

claims.claim: **S2 first line for idiopathic disease: oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, tapered slowly from 1-2 weeks to the lowest maintenance dose by 2-3 months;** if it flares during the taper, return at least to the previous dose. Complete plus partial response is sixty-five to 85%. Switch to second line if after 1 month the count is still above 1.5 per nL or the lowest maintenance dose exceeds 10 mg/day.
